title: Episode 159: Theodore Roosevelt: The Youngest President and the Square Deal (1901–1904)
description:
When William McKinley was assassinated in 1901, Republican party boss Mark Hanna exclaimed in horror: 'Now look! That damned cowboy is President of the United States!' At just forty-two years old, Theodore Roosevelt burst into the Executive Mansion like an uncontainable volcanic force, permanently revolutionizing the American presidency. Rejecting the passive, subservient role of Gilded Age executives, Roosevelt used the White House as a 'bully pulpit.' In 1902, when a massive anthracite coal strike threatened to freeze millions of Americans in their homes, Roosevelt shattered precedent by dragging arrogant coal barons and union leaders to the White House, threatening to seize the mines with the United States Army. Discover how TR dismantled J.P. Morgan's railroad monopoly and forged the immortal 'Square Deal.'

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we enter the whirlwind presidency of Theodore Roosevelt. A man of boundless physical energy, razor-sharp intellect, and fierce moral conviction, Roosevelt took the reins of a nation dominated by corporate monopolies and declared that the public interest was supreme. Here is George with the full story of TR and the dawn of the Square Deal.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: 'THAT DAMNED COWBOY'
When forty-two-year-old Theodore Roosevelt assumed the presidency on September 14, 1901, conservative Republican party bosses were gripped by sheer terror. A year earlier, New York political boss Thomas Platt had engineered Roosevelt's nomination for vice president specifically to bury the energetic young reformer in a powerless, ceremonial dead-end office. Senator Mark Hanna had warned his colleagues: 'Don't any of you realize that there's only one life between this madman and the White House?' Now, Hanna's nightmare had come true. Pacing the floor at McKinley's funeral, Hanna groaned aloud: 'Now look! That damned cowboy is President of the United States!'\n\nRoosevelt was unlike any man who had ever lived in the Executive Mansion. A sickly, asthmatic boy from a wealthy Manhattan family, Roosevelt had built an iron constitution through sheer willpower and boxing. He had been a Harvard scholar, a North Dakota cattle rancher, a New York City police commissioner, an assistant secretary of the navy, and the swashbuckling hero of San Juan Hill. He read a book a day, spoke with breathless, staccato enthusiasm, and greeted everyone with a ferocious grin of prominent white teeth. He possessed an almost mystical connection to the American people and an absolute conviction that the President of the United States was not a passive clerk of Congress, but a steward of the people, bound to do whatever the national interest required unless expressly forbidden by the Constitution.\n\nRoosevelt's kinetic energy and boundless curiosity electrified Washington, transforming the Executive Mansion into a vibrant center of intellectual, cultural, and political life.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE GREAT TRUST-BUSTING SHOCKWAVE
In early 1902, Roosevelt launched his opening thunderbolt against the unchecked power of corporate monopoly. In November 1901, the three most powerful financial titans in the world—J. Pierpont Morgan, James J. Hill, and Edward H. Harriman—had merged their giant western rail systems to create the Northern Securities Company. Capitalized at four hundred million dollars, Northern Securities created an absolute monopoly over all rail transportation from Chicago to the Pacific Ocean, dictating freight rates to western farmers and wiping out competition.\n\nWithout warning Wall Street or consulting congressional bosses, President Roosevelt ordered Attorney General Philander C. Knox to file a federal lawsuit under the long-dormant Sherman Antitrust Act to dissolve the Northern Securities Company. Wall Street was stunned into disbelief. J.P. Morgan, accustomed to treating American presidents as corporate subordinates, rushed to the White House in fury. Morgan looked at Roosevelt and said arrogantly: 'If we have done anything wrong, send your man to my man and they can fix it up.' Roosevelt smiled coldly and replied: 'That is not the way we do things here, Mr. Morgan. We don't want to fix it up; we want to stop it.' When Morgan asked if the President intended to attack his other companies, Roosevelt delivered an immortal reply: 'Only when we find they have done something wrong.'\n\nBy challenging J.P. Morgan's railroad monopoly, Roosevelt established that no private corporate empire, no matter how vast, was above the laws of the United States.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE ANTHRACITE COAL CRISIS OF 1902
In May 1902, a domestic catastrophe erupted that tested Roosevelt's philosophy of executive power to its limit. One hundred and forty thousand anthracite coal miners in northeastern Pennsylvania went on strike under the leadership of John Mitchell, president of the United Mine Workers. Anthracite was the essential heating fuel for the homes, hospitals, and schools of the entire American Northeast. The miners worked ten-hour days in dark, suffocating shafts, breathing in black coal dust and suffering constant roof cave-ins for wages that averaged less than six hundred dollars a year. They demanded a twenty percent wage increase, an eight-hour day, and formal union recognition.\n\nThe mine operators, led by George F. Baer, president of the Philadelphia and Reading Railway, refused to speak to Mitchell or submit the dispute to arbitration. Baer was a pious, arrogant corporate autocrat who scandalized the nation by publishing a public letter proclaiming: 'The rights and interests of the laboring man will be protected and cared for—not by the labor agitators, but by the Christian men of property to whom God has given control of the property rights of the country.' As summer turned to autumn, coal supplies dwindled to nothing, prices skyrocketed from five dollars to thirty dollars a ton, and schools in New York and Boston prepared to close for the winter. Riots were breaking out in major cities as cold weather approached.\n\nThe anthracite coal miners endured horrific working conditions and constant danger, making their disciplined struggle for fair wages a national moral cause.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: BREAKING PRECEDENT AT THE WHITE HOUSE
Under the strict constitutional view of prior Gilded Age presidents, a labor dispute between private corporations and their employees was none of the federal government's business, unless troops were needed to protect corporate property from strikers. But Theodore Roosevelt refused to let millions of American citizens freeze in their homes while arrogant coal barons played a game of corporate pride. On October 3, 1902, Roosevelt shattered all historical precedent by summoning both the mine operators and union leaders to a face-to-face conference in Washington.\n\nThe meeting was electric with tension. John Mitchell appeared quiet, dignified, and reasonable, offering to end the strike immediately if the operators would agree to let an impartial presidential commission arbitrate the dispute. George Baer and the operators reacted with furious insolence, berating the President of the United States for daring to invite 'anarchists and criminals' to the White House, and demanding that Roosevelt dispatch federal troops to shoot strikers and break the union. Roosevelt later admitted that the arrogance of the operators tested his temper almost beyond control: 'There was only one person in the room who behaved like a gentleman,' Roosevelt told friends, 'and that was John Mitchell.'\n\nRoosevelt's historic White House conference signaled a revolutionary departure from the past, declaring that the federal government was an independent advocate for the public welfare.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SECRET PLAN TO SEIZE THE MINES
When the operators stormed out of the White House, Roosevelt prepared a nuclear option. He summoned Lieutenant General John M. Schofield, former Commander-in-Chief of the United States Army, to a confidential meeting. Roosevelt informed Schofield that if the operators did not agree to arbitration within forty-eight hours, the President would issue an executive order declaring a national emergency. Schofield would lead ten thousand federal soldiers into the Pennsylvania coalfields, take physical control of the mines, run them as a federal receiver, and extract coal for the American people, completely dispossessing the owners.\n\nRoosevelt understood that this action had no statutory authority in American law, but he was completely prepared to execute it: 'I knew the coal barons would cry that this was unconstitutional,' Roosevelt wrote, 'and that I would be impeached. But I was determined that the coal would be mined, and the people would not freeze, and let the courts decide the legality afterward.' Roosevelt dispatched Secretary of War Elihu Root to New York to meet secretly with J.P. Morgan aboard Morgan's yacht Corsair. Root informed Morgan of the President's secret plan to seize the mines. Recognizing that Roosevelt was not bluffing, Morgan stepped in, twisting the arms of the reluctant mine operators and forcing them to accept presidential arbitration.\n\nGeneral Schofield's readiness to execute the President's orders demonstrated Roosevelt's absolute willingness to take unprecedented constitutional risks to protect the American people.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BIRTH OF THE SQUARE DEAL
On October 23, 1902, the five-month anthracite strike officially ended. The miners returned to the shafts, and trainloads of coal raced north just as the first winter blizzards struck New England. The presidential commission awarded the miners a ten percent wage increase and a nine-hour workday, while granting the operators a modest price increase. For the first time in American history, the federal government had intervened in a labor dispute not as the strikebreaking arm of corporate capital, but as an impartial umpire defending the public interest.\n\nFrom this triumph, Roosevelt coined the phrase that would define his entire domestic program: the 'Square Deal.' Speaking to an enormous crowd in Syracuse, New York, Roosevelt articulated his vision: 'All I ask is a square deal for every man. Give him a fair chance. Do not let him exploit his fellow citizens, and do not let his fellow citizens exploit him. We demand that big business give the people a square deal, and we demand that labor give big business a square deal.' Roosevelt had transformed the presidency into the supreme arbiter of American society.\n\nThe Square Deal redefined American conservatism by proving that government oversight of corporate monopoly was essential to preserve individual liberty and prevent socialist revolution.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE VERDICT OF THE SUPREME COURT
The climax of Roosevelt's first term arrived on March 14, 1904, when the Supreme Court of the United States handed down its historic decision in Northern Securities Co. v. United States. By a 5-to-4 majority, the Court ruled that the railroad holding company was an illegal monopoly and ordered it dissolved. The ruling was a seismic victory for executive authority, reversing decades of judicial decisions that had crippled the Sherman Antitrust Act. The federal government had proven that it was more powerful than Wall Street.\n\nRoosevelt was jubilant: 'The most powerful men in this country were held to account by the law,' he roared. 'We have established that the United States government is supreme over any corporation.' In November 1904, Roosevelt was reelected in a record-breaking popular landslide, carrying every northern and western state and winning the largest popular majority in American history up to that time. On election night, thirty-three years after entering the White House as an accidental president, Roosevelt smiled broadly at his wife Edith and announced: 'I am no longer a political accident.' The Progressive Era had found its champion.\n\nThe Supreme Court's dissolution of Northern Securities permanently affirmed the federal government's legal authority to regulate and dismantle monopolistic combinations.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Theodore Roosevelt's first term fundamentally transformed the relationship between the American presidency, corporate power, and the working public. By forging the Square Deal, he proved that democratic government possessed the moral authority to demand fairness from the mightiest monopolies. Next week, we conclude our portrait of TR with his historic second term: the construction of the Panama Canal, the voyage of the Great White Fleet, and the dramatic founding of the Bull Moose Party. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
